kyr_yeraishan_nishikyogoku_t.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision. This is a Japanese-style Chinese diner built on wheat: noodles, gyoza wrappers, and sauces thickened/seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce and likely doubanjiang. The signature mapo Tianjin rice rides on a mapo sauce that almost certainly contains wheat soy seasoning. There is no indication of gluten-free menus, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_yeraishan_nishikyogoku_t.vegan_detail: No vegan offering. The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward: pork features in the mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, and broths; dishes use animal-based stocks. Even otherwise plant-leaning items (fried rice, ankake) are cooked with meat/egg and shared woks. No vegetarian or vegan menu is advertised.
kyr_yeraishan_nishikyogoku_t.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu-Sun & holidays: 11:00-14:00 and 17:00-21:00 (lunch open also listed as 11:30 on some sources). Closed Wednesdays. Open during holidays, Golden Week and Obon. Some sources note occasional irregular closures.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood machi-chuka (Japanese-style Chinese) restaurant that has fed the Nishikyogoku district for roughly 40 years, just east of Hankyu Nishikyogoku Station on Hanayacho-dori. It draws a cross-section of locals, from solo diners on their lunch break to families, in a bright, big-windowed room with a warm, unpretentious feel.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, generous, affordable home-style Chinese cooking for the neighborhood — big portions, courteous service, and prices that keep regulars coming back day after day.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the maabo-tenshinhan (mapo Tianjin rice): a fluffy egg over rice blanketed in a generous, glossy mapo sauce. The sauce is built on house-made fermented black bean paste (豆鼓醤) and several chili pastes with ginger and plenty of garlic, given depth by coarsely minced salted fermented black beans (豆鼓の粒) and finished with house chili oil, with finely minced pork for richness — kept addictively savory rather than punishingly hot, served around 1,050 yen with soup and pickles.

anecdotes.text: The maabo-tenshinhan reportedly began life as a staff meal (まかない) before customers loved it enough that it became the house signature.
The mapo sauce poured over the Tianjin rice contains minced pork and aromatics but no tofu (豆腐は入っていない), giving it a concentrated, umami-rich punch against the mild egg-and-rice base.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based machi-chuka kitchen: noodles, gyoza, fried items and sauces share woks, fryers and prep surfaces, so cross-contamination with wheat is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chinese-diner cooking here relies on standard soy-based and bean-paste seasonings, which in Japan are wheat-containing; the signature mapo sauce is built on house doubanjiang and chili bean pastes.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork, egg and animal stocks run throughout the menu (mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, fried rice), cooked in shared woks, so no dish can be considered free of animal cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, at-home neighborhood Chinese diner where a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) goes a long way; English support is not advertised, so come with basic phrases or this guide.

kyr_chugoku_ryori_saikaku.gf_detail: A Sichuan Chinese kitchen built around wheat. The tantanmen and dumpling skins are wheat-flour, the chili/sesame tare and seasonings used in dishes like the mapo tofu lean on soy-based and bean-paste condiments that typically contain wheat, and there is no gluten-free menu or protocol. Not suitable for celiacs. A coeliac diner could ask whether any single rice- or vegetable-based plate could be prepared plainly, but cross-contact in a one-cook wok kitchen is unavoidable — treat as not GF-safe.
kyr_chugoku_ryori_saikaku.vegan_detail: Not a vegan specialist. The signature bowls (tantanmen, mapo tofu, boiled dumplings, sweet-and-sour pork) all use pork and/or animal-derived broth and condiments. There is no marked vegan option. Because it is a small a-la-carte Sichuan kitchen run by one chef, a vegan might be able to ask in advance for a plain vegetable stir-fry, but nothing is confirmed plant-based, so reserve and ask directly before relying on it.
kyr_chugoku_ryori_saikaku.hours_raw: Dinner 18:00-21:00 (L.O. ~20:30). Lunch not currently served (as of recent listing). Closed Sunday; Monday occasionally closed (~twice monthly); irregular temporary closures possible.

chef_bio.background: A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing — a cook with a reliable eye for ingredients who keeps the menu deliberately compact.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep the cooking simple and let quality ingredients carry it — the kind of place where, as one chef put it, everything you order somehow tastes good. Heat is balanced and aromatic rather than punishing.
chef_bio.specialty: Sichuan-style cooking pitched a notch upscale rather than fiery for its own sake: a fragrant tantanmen (the lunchtime dry 汁なし version is especially praised), a mapo tofu where the Sichuan pepper and chili oil are rounded out by the sweetness of the ground pork, plus boiled dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork.

anecdotes.text: Run entirely by one person, so the chef notes service may run slow — part of the charm of a true counter operation.
A fellow Kyoto chef of the same age describes the owner as a former market worker with a trustworthy eye for produce, whose relatively simple cooking nonetheless makes everything taste delicious.
Recognized as a Bib Gourmand selection in the Michelin Guide Kyoto 2023 (Nakagyo-ku Chinese).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles, wheat dumpling skins, and wheat-containing Chinese seasonings (soy/bean pastes) are central to the menu and share a single one-cook wok station; assume heavy gluten cross-contact.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sichuan dishes such as the mapo tofu and the chili/sesame tantanmen tare rely on soy- and fermented-bean-based seasonings that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature dishes use pork and animal-based broth/condiments throughout; no dedicated plant-based prep is indicated, and a single chef cooks everything in shared woks.

positives.text: Tiny 14-seat counter with one attentive chef-owner who takes reservations, so allergy questions can be raised directly when booking — though no formal allergen handling is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run Sichuan counter where one chef cooks everything, so Japanese (or a Japanese-speaking companion) and a prior reservation make for the smoothest visit; come ready to be patient and order in Japanese.

kyr_ramen_daisenso_kyoto_kaw.gf_detail: A wheat-noodle ramen specialist whose signature bowls are built on soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat. Both the noodles and the seasoning base contain gluten, and no gluten-free menu or noodle option is indicated. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_ramen_daisenso_kyoto_kaw.vegan_detail: All four signature bowls are animal-based: the broths are made from chicken bones (Nagoya Cochin), scallop, and fish/dashi elements, and chashu (pork) is a centerpiece. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
kyr_ramen_daisenso_kyoto_kaw.hours_raw: 11:00-00:00 (L.O. 23:30), open daily. (Some local listings note 11:00-22:30; the official store information on the listing shows until midnight.)

chef_bio.background: Ramen Daisenso ("Ramen World War") is the Kyoto outpost of the acclaimed Osaka ramen group behind Jinrui Mina Menrui, the much-queued shop that turned shoyu ramen into something theatrical. This branch opened in October 2022 on the first floor of a renovated Kawaramachi building (formerly a sushi restaurant) and marked the group's first move into Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: A noodle-first house: the noodle-making room is visible from the street, signalling pride in house-made noodles, paired with generous service — diners can add up to five chashu slices and get a free half-portion noodle refill (kaedama).
chef_bio.specialty: The flagship bowl is the Kansai-dashi shoyu ramen named 'Pistol' (ピストル) — a clear, light-bodied shoyu broth built on Nagoya Cochin chicken bones and scallop, with deep umami and a faint natural sweetness. The lineup of four soy-based bowls also includes 'Heiwa' (平和), 'Sabita Katana' (錆びた刀, a brothless/soupless shoyu), and 'Jiyu' (自由).

anecdotes.text: The shop names its bowls after evocative wartime-and-peace imagery — 'Pistol,' 'Peace,' 'Rusty Sword,' 'Freedom' — fitting the playful 'Ramen World War' branding of the group.
Its arrival was billed as the Osaka queue-shop's first expansion into Kyoto, opening on 4 October 2022.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the kitchen is built around wheat-based shoyu tare; gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Signature bowls are Kansai-dashi shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen; Japanese shoyu tare is brewed from wheat, so the seasoning base contains gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are made from chicken bone and scallop with fish/dashi elements, and chashu pork is central — no plant-based option and pervasive animal-product use.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, queue-friendly counter-and-table ramen shop in central Kawaramachi; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the photo menu will carry you through ordering.

kyr_jinrui_mina_menrui_tsuke.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The house dipping noodles are 全粒粉入りの極太麺 — extra-thick wheat (whole-grain) noodles — and the rich pork-bone-and-seafood dipping broth almost certainly carries wheat through the tare. There is no gluten-free noodle or dedicated preparation. Anyone with celiac disease or a wheat allergy should not eat here.
kyr_jinrui_mina_menrui_tsuke.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The entire menu is built on a 豚骨魚介 (pork-bone and fish/seafood) broth, with a pork rice bowl (豚丼) as the main side. No vegetable or plant-based broth option is offered.

chef_bio.background: This is the Kyoto branch of 人類みな麺類, a tsukemen specialty offshoot of one of Osaka's most famous ramen brands. The original 人類みな麺類 opened in Nishinakajima, Osaka in 2012 and built a reputation for weekend lines of fifty-plus people. The dedicated tsukemen shop launched as a new sub-brand in Osaka's Yodogawa ward in April 2025; this Kyoto-shiyakusho-mae location opened on September 1, 2025 as its second outpost, just steps from Kawaramachi-dori.
chef_bio.philosophy: The brand name 人類みな麺類 — playfully glossed in English as 'Human beings, everybody noodles' — captures founder Matsumura's idea that noodles are something all of humanity shares. The kitchen states its aim plainly: to deliver the highest performance it can currently offer and to keep building the finest shop it can.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick whole-grain wheat dipping noodles served with a rich, mellow pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) dipping broth lifted with scallion-oil richness. The signature lineup is three broths — 原点 (the 'origin'), macro, and micro — with noodle portions of 200g, 300g and 400g all at the same price. The Kyoto-only bowl is the 九条ネギつけ麺, finished with fragrant local Kujo green onion. A small pork rice bowl and a finishing-rice option round out the dip.

anecdotes.text: Matsumura has said the name was born when he was a high-schooler: after a part-time shift he went for ramen with friends, warmed his hands on the bowl, and the thought struck him — 'humanity is all noodles' (人類はみな麺類や) — which became the name of his first shop.
The dipping noodles are made extremely long — eaters use scissors at the table to cut them as they go — a hallmark carried over from the tsukemen brand.
The Kyoto-exclusive 九条ネギ tsukemen was announced as the local-only special when the shop opened on September 1, 2025.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, popular tsukemen counter where a few words of Japanese and following the eat-as-you-go rhythm (the noodles are very long and you cut them with scissors at the table) will make ordering smooth.

kyr_hakata_nagahama_ramen_mi.gf_detail: This is a Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen shop built around wheat noodles (ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles) in a pork-bone broth, with kaedama (noodle refills) as a core part of the experience. There are no gluten-free noodle or broth options, and no dedicated gluten-free preparation. Not suitable for celiac diners. No allergen handling information was found.
kyr_hakata_nagahama_ramen_mi.vegan_detail: The entire concept is a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth — the shop's identity is its pork broth, kept going continuously. There is essentially one ramen, animal-based, with toppings like chashu (pork). No vegan or even vegetarian bowl is offered.

chef_bio.background: 博多長浜ラーメン みよし opened in 1983 (昭和58年) in Kyoto's Kiyamachi/Sanjo entertainment district and has become an old-school local institution — '京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない' (there is no one in Kyoto who doesn't know its name). For roughly four decades it has carried the same Hakata Nagahama taste, its small open counter running late into the night.
chef_bio.philosophy: A purist, no-frills tonkotsu shop: keep the pork-bone broth going, add nothing unnecessary, and let each diner build their own flavor with the tabletop condiments. Regulars even treat certain moves (like adding pepper or curry powder) as 'forbidden,' and finishing by pouring extra broth over rice is part of the ritual.
chef_bio.specialty: Essentially one bowl done one way: Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen — a clean, gently sweet pork-bone broth paired with ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles. Diners customize at the table with around eleven free toppings (beni-shoga pickled ginger, coarse ichimi chili, tenkasu tempura scraps, sesame, etc.) and can order kaedama noodle refills, which is treated as part of doing Nagahama ramen 'your way.'

anecdotes.text: Often cited as a place 'everyone in Kyoto knows' (京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない) — an old-establishment late-night ramen counter running since 1983.

Famous celebrity regular: the gourmet entertainer GACKT, who reportedly rarely eats ramen, is said to have been a loyal customer since his university days and to finish with extra broth poured over rice (替えスープ).
Recommended order from fans: ramen with 'barikata' (extra-firm) noodles, customized with beni-shoga, coarse ichimi, and tenkasu — with pepper and curry powder considered the 'forbidden' moves (禁じ手).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core menu is wheat ramen noodles in a shared tonkotsu broth with kaedama (noodle refills), so a single shared noodle/broth workflow — high cross-contamination risk for gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shop is built on a continuously simmered pork-bone broth; there is no separate non-animal broth, so all bowls share an animal-based base.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, retro 16-seat counter-only late-night ramen counter in Kyoto's Kiyamachi nightlife district run by a longtime local family; little to no English, food-ticket ordering, and best approached with basic Japanese and casual ramen-counter etiquette.

kyr_menkiya_kyoto_mibu_honte.gf_detail: A wheat-noodle ramen shop built on a pork-bone-and-back-fat soy-sauce broth. The thin noodles are wheat, the soy-sauce tare is virtually certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the broth is pork-derived — none of which is celiac-safe. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, tare, or menu item, no dedicated equipment, and shared pots/cooking surfaces make cross-contamination unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_menkiya_kyoto_mibu_honte.vegan_detail: The entire concept is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and back-fat broth with pork chashu and toppings such as a boiled egg; sides include karaage and gyoza. There is no vegan or even vegetarian ramen on offer and no plant-based broth alternative noted. Not suitable for vegans.

chef_bio.background: A late-night neighborhood ramen counter sitting right inside the Shijo-Omiya shopping arcade, a few steps from Hankyu Omiya Station. It runs from late morning straight through to around 2 AM, shifting from a lunchtime rush, to evening drinkers ordering sides with beer, to a sudden surge of customers chasing the last trains.
chef_bio.philosophy: The whole shop is built around one idea — 毎日でも食べられるラーメン, 'ramen you could eat every day' — leaning on accessible, balanced flavor rather than heavy gimmickry, using selected ingredients like Kyoto Tanba highland pork and Kujo negi.
chef_bio.specialty: Their core bowl is a classic Kyoto-style se-abura shoyu (back-fat soy-sauce) tonkotsu ramen: a pork-bone broth finished with back fat over thin, easy-slurping noodles, topped with chashu, with branch menus extending to shoyu-pork, chashu-men, and a miso ramen made with miso shipped from Hokkaido.

anecdotes.text: A boiled egg comes with the bowl and a cup of cold matcha is served as an after-meal gesture — small touches that fit the everyday-comfort idea.

It is documented as a 深夜も賑わう地元の繁盛店 — a locally bustling shop that stays busy late, with after-work diners ordering karaage and gyoza alongside an economical fried-rice set, then a last-train crowd queuing outside.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles, a wheat-based soy-sauce tare, and shared cooking equipment make this unsafe for celiac diners; no gluten-free handling is indicated.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature bowl is a back-fat shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen; the tare is virtually certainly standard wheat-containing shoyu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone and back fat with pork chashu; no vegan or vegetarian option is offered, so all bowls share an animal-based base.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, locals-first neighborhood ramen counter where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will carry you through, though detailed dietary questions in English may be hard.

kyr_kyoto_kitayama_motomachi.gf_detail: This is a traditional soy sauce ramen shop: wheat noodles in a pork-and-chicken-bone broth seasoned with a tamari-style soy sauce tare, which is wheat-based. There is no gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no published allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_kyoto_kitayama_motomachi.vegan_detail: The broth is built on pork bones blended with chicken bones, and the signature bowls feature back fat, beef tendon and pork toppings. A "vegetable ramen" (野菜らーめん) is on the menu but it is served in the same animal-based broth, so it is not vegan or vegetarian. No plant-based broth is offered.
kyr_kyoto_kitayama_motomachi.notes: [Mom & Pop] The shop traces its roots to a Chinese-noodle (中華そば) food cart in Kyoto's Kitayama Kitamachi that ran for roughly 50 years before settling into a storefront in the Shijo Karasuma area. chef_bio.background: The shop traces its roots to a Chinese-noodle (中華そば) food cart that stood in a parking lot in Kyoto's Kitayama Shinmachi (北山新町); the business marks 創業50年 (fifty years since its founding) and carries that cart's dark soy-sauce flavor forward into its Shijo-Karasuma storefront.
chef_bio.philosophy: Carry forward the single signature flavor born on the old cart while serving generous, satisfying bowls late into the night for the downtown crowd.
chef_bio.specialty: A rich, dark soy-sauce ramen made with a tamari-style soy sauce of the kind traditionally used for eel sauce (うなぎのタレ), plus a Kyoto-style back-fat (背脂) soy sauce variant with fat drizzled over the top. Beef-tendon ramen (牛すじらーめん), made with sweet-savory domestic lean beef tendon, is a signature bowl.

anecdotes.text: The current shop grew out of a 中華そば food cart that operated in a parking lot in Kyoto's Kitayama Shinmachi, and it still builds its bowls on that same dark soy-sauce flavor (創業50年 屋台の味).
Its calling card is a 'concentrated soy sauce ramen' using a tamari-style soy sauce, offered alongside a Kyoto-style back-fat soy sauce version.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is seasoned with a tamari-style soy sauce tare, which is a wheat-based fermented seasoning.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local late-night ramen counter where ordering is simple but staff and signage are Japanese-only, so a little Japanese or pointing at the menu helps.

kyr_ramen_ten_honten.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. Ramen uses wheat noodles and a wheat-based soy (shoyu) tare; the kitchen also fries chicken karaage. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is indicated, and cross-contamination is unavoidable for a celiac.
kyr_ramen_ten_honten.vegan_detail: No vegan options. Broth is pork-bone based; ramen is topped with sliced pork. No plant-based ramen or sides are offered.

kyr_ramen_ten_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A neighborhood ramen institution that has been running since the Showa era — locals describe it as a 30-plus-year veteran shop that relocated to its current spot a few years back and quickly filled its 37 seats again at both lunch and late night.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood ramen institution that has been running since the Showa era — locals describe it as a 30-plus-year veteran shop that relocated to its current Yamashina spot (from beneath the Tokaido Shinkansen overpass) a few years back and quickly filled its 37 seats again at both lunch and late night.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, generous everyday ramen for the neighborhood, served late into the night.
chef_bio.specialty: A classic Kyoto bowl: a light yet satisfying soy-seasoned pork-bone broth, paired with firm, snappy straight noodles topped with thin-sliced pork, bamboo shoots, bean sprouts and green onion. The bargain A-set adds a big bowl of rice and fried chicken.

anecdotes.text: Regulars rave that the firm straight noodles are quintessentially Kyoto — 'この麺嫌いな京都人おらんやろ' (no Kyoto person could dislike this noodle) — and that the spicy miso served alongside pairs beautifully with the broth.
It is one of the rare Yamashina spots open until 2 a.m., making it a go-to for late-night eaters.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the shop also fries chicken karaage, so gluten exposure is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a soy (shoyu) tare ramen; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone based and ramen is topped with pork, so no dish is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, no-frills local ramen counter where Japanese will smooth ordering; little to no English is expected, but pointing at the menu works for a simple bowl.

kyr_ryumon_uzumasa.gf_detail: A neighborhood Sichuan/Chinese restaurant. The signature 鶏肉の葱油かけそば and other noodle dishes are built on wheat noodles, and Chinese cooking here leans heavily on soy sauce, oyster/bean-based sauces, and shared wok/fryer surfaces. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac diners; assume cross-contamination throughout.
kyr_ryumon_uzumasa.vegan_detail: A meat-and-seafood-forward Chinese kitchen — the house specialty centers on fried chicken and chicken oil, and stocks/sauces are animal-based. No vegan menu or documented plant-based broth. While a few vegetable stir-fries (e.g. spicy eggplant) exist on the menu, they are not prepared vegan (soy/oyster-style sauces, shared woks, likely meat-based stock), so no reliable vegan option can be confirmed.

chef_bio.background: 龍門 is a small Kyoto chain of authentic Sichuan / neighborhood-Chinese (町中華) restaurants run by 株式会社長城, with the Honten near Sanjo-Higashioji and branches in Okazaki and here in Uzumasa, in Ukyo-ku near the Arashiyama (Randen) line and JR Uzumasa. It has built a reputation as the kind of unpretentious place that draws not just Kyotoites but diners from across Japan and even visitors from China itself, seeking the real thing at gentle prices.
chef_bio.philosophy: Serve genuine, full-flavored Chinese cooking — fragrant with Sichuan pepper and star anise — at everyday prices in a lively, no-frills room.
chef_bio.specialty: The house signature is 鶏肉の葱油かけそば — crisp fried chicken over straight medium-thick noodles in a chicken-oil-rich bowl, finished with scallions and chili and a pour of sizzling hot oil. Alongside it, the spicy stir-fried eggplant (茄子のピリ辛炒め) is often called a dish that all but represents the restaurant.

anecdotes.text: 龍門 is described as a 町中華 popular not only with Kyoto locals but with diners from all over Japan and even Chinese visitors from the mainland, who come for an authentic taste.

The 鶏肉の葱油かけそば is an original noodle dish made with authentic Chinese technique — crisp fried chicken and chicken oil in the broth over straight medium-thick noodles, topped with scallion and chili and finished with hot oil.
The spicy eggplant stir-fry is singled out as a dish that it would be no exaggeration to call representative of 龍門.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Signature and most dishes use wheat noodles and wheat-based Chinese sauces; shared woks and a shared fryer mean pervasive gluten cross-contact. No gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Chinese cooking here relies on soy sauce and bean/oyster-style sauces, which are wheat-containing; no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward (the signature bowl centers on fried chicken and chicken oil); vegetable dishes are cooked in shared woks likely with animal-based stock/sauces, so no reliable vegan preparation can be confirmed.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, locals-and-visitors neighborhood Chinese spot where staff may speak Chinese as much as Japanese; a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will carry you, but expect little English.

kyr_yumin.gf_detail: Not safe for gluten-free or celiac diners. The entire concept is abura-soba built on thick house-made wheat noodles (made from 100% "オーション" strong wheat flour), dressed in a soy/oil tare that is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, with pork back fat. There is no published allergen information and no gluten-free option. Avoid if you require celiac-level safety.
kyr_yumin.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. This is a Jiro-style abura-soba shop centered on pork back fat (背脂), wheat noodles, and a savory oil/soy tare; standard toppings include raw or soft-boiled egg, pork fat, mentaiko mayo, and cream cheese. No plant-based or vegetarian bowl is offered.
kyr_yumin.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00, 17:30-22:30 (Fri close 22:00). Note: opening-period hours, subject to change — confirm via Instagram.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Sakyo-ku, Tanaka Monzencho), as a spin-off of the Ichijoji ramen shop びし屋
chef_bio.background: 油珉 (Yumin) opened on October 10, 2025 in the Hyakumanben university quarter, just north of the Hyakumanben intersection and a short walk from Demachiyanagi and Kyoto University. It is the second brand of びし屋 (Bishiya), the popular, queue-forming ramen shop in Kyoto's Ichijoji — the staff here are the Bishiya team, who set out to make a dedicated abura-soba (brothless mixed noodle) specialist for the student neighborhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: Affordable, high-volume, punchy noodles aimed squarely at hungry students — リーズナブル prices and a 'wash-wash' (ワシワシ) chewy texture with the wallop of back fat.
chef_bio.specialty: Jiro-style abura-soba. The standout is the 背脂ヤサイあぶらそば (back-fat & vegetable abura-soba) — extra-thick house-made noodles milled from 100% strong 'オーション' wheat flour, piled with pork back fat, vegetables, menma and naruto, finished tableside with minced garlic and chopped onion. The lineup is three bowls: あぶらそば (750 yen), 辛味あぶらそば (spicy, 850 yen) and 背脂ヤサイあぶらそば (850 yen), with portions scalable from 180g up to a 540g triple.

anecdotes.text: Visitors realized the people running it were the crew from the famous Ichijoji ramen shop びし屋 — 「中の人たちは一乗寺のラーメン店『びし屋』の方々でした」.
The thick house noodles are described as 'オーション100％の極太麺' with a snappy 'ブリンブリン' and chewy 'ワシワシ' texture and strong wheat flavor — the heart of its 二郎系 character.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Built entirely on wheat: thick house-made noodles from 100% strong wheat flour ('オーション100％の極太麺'), in a shared boiling-water/noodle workflow typical of a noodle shop.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dressing is a strong soy-based oil tare with prominent garlic ('醤油ベースのオイルだれ'), which in this style is virtually always wheat-containing shoyu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls center on pork back fat (背脂) and the standard toppings include raw/soft-boiled egg, pork fat, mentaiko mayo and cream cheese; no plant-based preparation is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, student-oriented Jiro-style noodle counter with a ticket-vending-machine ordering system and no published English support, so basic Japanese (or the menu photos) helps; the casual, generous portions make it easy and welcoming once you've chosen.

kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_2_karasu.gf_detail: This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use medium-thin straight wheat noodles in a soy (shoyu) tare broth, so both the noodles and the seasoning base contain wheat/gluten. No gluten-free noodles or menu are mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_2_karasu.vegan_detail: The signature bowls are built on a chicken (Nagoya Cochin) and dried-bonito broth and are topped with thin-sliced pork belly chashu. The soup is animal-based and there is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu.
kyr_ramen_mugyu_vol_2_karasu.notes: [Mom & Pop] Tucked into a narrow alley just off Takoyakushi-dori near Karasuma, Ramen Mugyu Vol.2 is the second outpost of the original Ramen Mugyu, which began in the Maruyama area. The shop occupies a converted townhouse-style space with a long counter and a relaxed, almost izakaya-like fe

chef_bio.background: Tucked into a narrow alley just off Takoyakushi-dori near Karasuma, Ramen Mugyu Vol.2 is the second outpost of the original Ramen Mugyu, whose Vol.1 shop is in the Enmachi (円町) area. The shop occupies a converted townhouse-style space with a long counter and a relaxed, almost izakaya-like feel; guests are handed paper aprons on arrival to keep the splatter off.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen leans into a clean, sharp Kyoto-style shoyu profile — proper soy richness with a subtle seafood undertone and a clear chicken backbone — that diners have compared to the old-school Kyoto tradition of Shinpuku Saikan.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the "Onibara Kuro" (鬼腹黒) shoyu ramen: a soy-forward broth built on purebred Nagoya Cochin chicken (純系名古屋コーチン) and aged dried bonito (本枯れ節), brightened with a re-steeped premium soy sauce from Ehime's Kajita shoyu, and finished with medium-thin straight noodles and a fan of extremely thin-sliced pork belly chashu that blankets the bowl. A lighter "Onibara Shiro" (白, white) version and a rich chicken soba (濃厚鶏そば / nōkō torisoba) round out the lineup.

anecdotes.text: Regulars and reviewers liken the soy-based, crisp and salty broth to the venerable Kyoto institution Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館).
Diners are given a paper apron on entry to protect against splashes, and the counter stretches lengthwise with a notably wide, open kitchen.
The bowl is topped with very thin slices of pork belly chashu that, despite covering the whole surface, stay light on the palate.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature bowls use a soy-sauce (shoyu) based tare, and conventional shoyu is brewed with wheat — this is the seasoning backbone of the broth.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual neighborhood counter ramen shop tucked in an alley; a friendly greeting and pointing at the bowl you want will carry you through, though staff likely speak little English.

kyr_kirameki_no_aozora.gf_detail: This is a standard ramen and mazesoba shop. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles, with a wheat-based shoyu/tare element and a rich chicken broth, so they are not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners. There is no gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no indication of any allergen-handling or dedicated preparation. Even the "shio" (salt) version of the chicken paitan is served over wheat noodles. Treat this as not gluten-free.
kyr_kirameki_no_aozora.vegan_detail: The house style is built around a thick chicken (tori-paitan) broth, with chicken chashu and other meat toppings; the Taiwan mazesoba and dan-dan dishes use minced meat. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on offer and no plant-based broth alternative. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

chef_bio.background: キラメキノ青空 is a Kyoto-grown ramen and mazesoba brand run by the Kirameki Group (キラメキノ未来株式会社), known across Kansai as one of the pioneers of Taiwan-style mazesoba. The group operates a spread of shops through Kyoto — in student and downtown neighborhoods such as Yamanouchi (山ノ内) and Tanaka near Kyoto University — and out into Osaka, Shiga and Nara as part of a stated '30-store project'; this Shijo-Muromachi shop (下京区鶏鉾町), a short walk from Shijo-Karasuma, opened as one of its newer locations.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans into bold, concentrated flavor and customization: diners are encouraged to tune their bowl with a lemon wedge and the tabletop condiments to shift the heavy chicken broth across the meal.
chef_bio.specialty: A thick, intensely rich tori-paitan (chicken white broth) ramen, offered in both a 'shio no Kirameki' salt version and a shoyu version, built on chicken paitan with niboshi and topped with chashu, menma and green onion, with a lemon wedge for mid-bowl 味変. The kitchen also turns out Taiwan mazesoba and a newer dan-dan mazesoba.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers compare the broth's density to Tenkaiippin's famous pottage-thick soup — 'スープは天下一品みたいなドロドロのポタージュ系' — a heavy, almost gloopy chicken paitan (ぼってりと重い鶏白湯スープ) that rewards using the table condiments and lemon to vary the flavor.
The shop draws a young crowd into the evening — patrons arriving even before 11 p.m. (23時前でも若者がどんどんやってくる) — with a touch-screen ticket vending machine set up outside the storefront for ordering.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard ramen and mazesoba shop: bowls are built on wheat noodles with a wheat-based shoyu/tare element, so wheat is a core ingredient throughout the menu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is built around chicken broth and meat toppings (chicken chashu, minced meat in the mazesoba), so there is heavy meat contact across all preparations.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, fast-paced late-night ramen spot with a self-service ticket machine and Japanese-only menu, so a little guidance on ordering helps, but no special etiquette is required.

kyr_daiichi_asahi_katsura_te.gf_detail: This is a classic Kyoto-style chuka-soba shop: the ramen is built on wheat noodles in a pork-bone-and-soy-sauce (shoyu) broth, and the soy-sauce tare is almost certainly wheat-based. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated handling, or allergen accommodation is indicated anywhere. Not safe for celiac diners.
kyr_daiichi_asahi_katsura_te.vegan_detail: The house broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base finished with soy sauce, and signature bowls are topped with chashu/roast pork. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen offering noted; even a plain bowl would carry the pork broth. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_daiichi_asahi_katsura_te.hours_raw: Tue-Sun 11:00-24:00 (L.O. 23:30), closed Mon. Some sources note it stays open until around 3:00 in the morning.
kyr_daiichi_asahi_katsura_te.notes: [Mom & Pop] A Katsura-neighborhood outpost of the long-running Kyoto ramen name Daiichi Asahi, this shop carries on a recipe and reputation built over more than fifty years, passed down through the noren-wake tradition of opening a branch under the founding house's name and methods.

chef_bio.background: A Katsura-neighborhood outpost of the long-running Kyoto ramen name Daiichi Asahi, this shop carries on a recipe and reputation built over more than fifty years, passed down through the noren-wake tradition of opening a branch under the founding house's name and methods.
chef_bio.philosophy: Despite the richness of the pork-and-soy foundation, the broth leans on plenty of simmered vegetable stock to finish clean and light on the palate, the balance Daiichi Asahi is known for. Long daily hours (to around 3am) and a no-frills counter make it the kind of place the neighborhood drops into at any hour, including after a night out.
chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-style chuka-soba: thin straight noodles in a deeply flavored shoyu broth set on a pork-bone base, crowned with sliced roast pork and a generous heap of green onion. The hearty Special Ramen is the bowl regulars reach for, and the house yakimeshi (fried rice) has its own devoted following.

anecdotes.text: The shop is a noren-wake branch of a Kyoto ramen house with over fifty years of history, carrying the name and recipe of the original.
Regulars single out the fried rice (yakimeshi) as exceptionally good alongside the ramen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: gourpass confirms a noren-wake branch of a 50-plus-year Kyoto ramen house, pork-bone/rich-shoyu broth with abundant vegetable stock, Special Ramen (¥650), yakimeshi (¥450), 24 seats, and hours to 3am near Katsura Station.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is described as a pork-bone base seasoned with a deeply flavored soy sauce (shoyu), which in this style is virtually always wheat-containing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base and bowls are topped with roast pork, so animal products are integral to the dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, cash-only neighborhood ramen counter where a few words of Japanese will go a long way and an English menu should not be assumed.

kyr_ramen_yatai.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. The core dish is Taiwan ramen built on wheat ramen noodles in a pork/minced-meat-and-chili broth, and the menu (gyoza, fried chicken "Apache," yakitori) is wheat- and soy-sauce-heavy. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_ramen_yatai.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The signature Taiwan ramen relies on minced pork and a meat-based broth, and the broader menu centers on chicken, pork, and seafood items. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is advertised.
kyr_ramen_yatai.hours_raw: 11:00-14:00 / 17:00-23:00 (Tabelog); some listings show evening close at 22:30. Closed Tuesdays.

chef_bio.background: らーめん屋台 (Ramen Yatai) started in the Yoshoin neighborhood of Kyoto's Minami Ward and relocated in April 2025 to the Taishogun area (Kita Ward) near Kitano-Hakubaicho, in the direction of Kinkaku-ji and Enmachi. It is a small, independent neighborhood ramen-and-izakaya hybrid.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is 台湾ラーメン (Taiwan ramen): a spicy bowl where heat and umami intertwine over a deeply rich broth, finished with garlic, chili, minced meat, and Chinese chives (nira) that you mix thoroughly before eating. Its other famous item is the 'アパッチ (Apache)' — crispy-outside, juicy-inside deep-fried chicken-wing pieces with a lingering spicy seasoning, said to pair perfectly with both beer and the Taiwan ramen.

anecdotes.text: The shop relocated from its original Yoshoin location to the Taishogun/Kitano-Hakubaicho area in April 2025.
Beyond ramen the kitchen serves gyoza, yakitori, oden, and assorted small plates with alcohol, giving it a casual izakaya feel.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the April 2025 relocation from Yoshoin (Minami-ku) to 北区大将軍東鷹司町 near Kitano-Hakubaicho, the Taiwan ramen and Apache (手羽中唐揚げ) specialties, and gyoza/yakitori/oden izakaya offerings.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the shop is described as welcoming to families, couples, and solo diners, so non-Japanese-speaking visitors should manage comfortably.

kyr_chugoku_ryori_kuretake.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The ramen and tantanmen are built on wheat noodles, and the broths use a soy-sauce (wheat shoyu) and sesame base over chicken/pork/vegetable stock; the sake-lees ramen dissolves sake lees into a soy-ramen base and is topped with char siu. As a town Chinese kitchen, gyoza, fried items, and stir-fries all involve shared wheat/soy. No celiac handling indicated. A coeliac diner should not eat here without a verified, separately-prepared dish — and none is documented.
kyr_chugoku_ryori_kuretake.vegan_detail: Not a vegan place. The signature noodles use chicken/pork/vegetable broth and char siu pork, and the tantanmen is topped with sweet-miso minced meat. Some vegetable dishes (e.g., a mixed-vegetable set, mapo tofu) exist but are not stated to be meat/animal-free and a shared meat kitchen applies. Vegans would need to ask, with no documented vegan option.
kyr_chugoku_ryori_kuretake.hours_raw: 11:00–21:00 (Tabelog); some sources list 11:00–23:00 (L.O. 22:30) with through-service / weekday lunch specials roughly 11:00–14:00. Confirm directly.

chef_bio.background: A long-loved neighborhood Chinese kitchen (町中華) standing at the northwest corner of Oote-dori and Kyomachi-dori, right in front of Fushimi-Momoyama Station and a minute from Momoyama-Goryomae. It has become a fixture for locals who come for serious cooking served in an unfussy, drop-in setting, with a wood-floored dining room and an adjacent same-name café for Western dishes and coffee.
chef_bio.philosophy: No flashiness, just reliable depth — whatever you order is dependably good, and the heat is kept mild enough that even spice-averse diners can enjoy the tantanmen.
chef_bio.specialty: Sesame-forward tantanmen and, in the cold months, the house's signature sake-lees ramen and sake-lees tantanmen — a nod to Fushimi's sake-brewing heritage. The sake-lees ramen dissolves sake lees into a clear (清湯) chicken-, pork- and vegetable-based soup, finished with char siu and vegetables; the sake-lees tantanmen layers the lees over a rich house-sesame paste and house chili oil, topped with sweet-miso minced pork.

anecdotes.text: The winter-only sake-lees bowls (roughly November to early March, tracking the new-sake brewing season) use sake lees from Fushimi's breweries to add a smooth, warming, complex umami — described as rich and body-warming ('身体ポカポカ').
Locals describe it as a long-established town Chinese place beloved in the neighborhood, where the mapo tofu and tantanmen carry a deep sesame aroma without being overly spicy.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: totteoki and kyotopi confirm the Fushimi-Momoyama location, clear (清湯) sake-lees ramen and sake-lees tantanmen available roughly Nov–early March using Fushimi sake lees (Tamanohikari), the rich-sesame-paste tantanmen with sweet-miso minced pork, mild spice, and the body-warming quality; freelife confirms the beloved 町中華 status and sesame-forward mapo tofu/tantanmen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Noodles are wheat and the broths use soy sauce (wheat shoyu) plus a sesame base; the kitchen is a general town-Chinese kitchen making gyoza, fried rice and stir-fries, so wheat and soy are pervasive. No gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The sake-lees ramen is explicitly a soy-sauce ramen (醤油ラーメン) with sake lees dissolved in, indicating standard wheat-containing soy sauce in the tare.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature bowls use chicken/pork/vegetable broth and char siu, and the tantanmen is topped with minced-meat miso; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local town-Chinese spot with no English presence indicated, so a little Japanese or pointing at the menu will make ordering smooth.

kyr_menya_craze_mibu_honten.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The bowls are built on wheat noodles (from the Teigaku/棣鄂 noodle maker), a tonkotsu broth finished with what is almost certainly a wheat-based shoyu tare, and a flour-dredged karaage side. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation or separate handling, so this is not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_menya_craze_mibu_honten.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is an ultra-rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth, with chashu, marinated egg, and other animal toppings; even the side dishes are meat. No plant-based broth or noodle option is offered.
kyr_menya_craze_mibu_honten.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 / 17:00-22:00 (last order 30 min before each close), closed Tue (also irregular days off - check Instagram)

chef_bio.background: 麺屋 栩羚廚（くれいず）opened on September 12, 2024 on Kouin-dori between Shijo-Omiya and Sanjo-Senbon, an area of central Kyoto in the middle of a wave of new ramen openings. It is a small, design-conscious counter shop that put down roots fast: within months it had drawn a steady following and, in February 2025, opened a second branch in Tokyo's Nakameguro.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'material-commitment' approach paired with careful plating — a richly concentrated pork broth that locals rate among the thickest in Kyoto yet keeps the typical tonkotsu off-smell in check, served with attentive hospitality in a stylish little room.
chef_bio.specialty: The house specialty is an extremely thick, creamy Kyoto-pork tonkotsu. Two core styles anchor the menu — a 濃厚豚骨醤油 (rich tonkotsu-shoyu) and the 極濃豚骨, a paste-thick 'doro-kei' broth poured with a layer of flavorful tare on top that you stir in before eating; a 旨辛豚骨 spiced with ichimi togarashi sits between them. The signature bowl is the limited 極濃豚骨味玉 (¥1,250), built on flat, chewy wheat noodles from the respected Teigaku (棣鄂) noodle maker and finished with squared-cut chashu, a marinated egg, bamboo shoots, and scallion.

anecdotes.text: Diners are offered complimentary burnt-garlic oil (焦がしにんにく油) to add partway through the bowl, deepening the umami and giving the broth a second character mid-meal.
The shop's popularity grew quickly after its September 2024 opening, leading to a Tokyo (Nakameguro) branch in February 2025.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyo-soku confirms the Sept 12 2024 opening on Kouin-dori, the ドロドロ-thick broth rated top-class in Kyoto, the 極濃豚骨味玉 (¥1,250) on 棣鄂 noodles, and the burnt-garlic oil; noodlers confirms the Feb 2025 Tokyo Nakameguro second branch.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls use wheat ramen noodles (from the Teigaku/棣鄂 maker) cooked in shared boiling water, and the karaage side is flour-dredged and deep-fried; no gluten-free handling is indicated.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The core 濃厚豚骨醤油 and the tare layered over the 極濃豚骨 are soy-sauce based, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every bowl is built on a pork-bone broth with animal toppings (chashu, egg); there is no separate vegan prep area or plant-based option.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny eight-seat counter shop run on a ticket-vending-machine system, so you can order with almost no Japanese, though a friendly greeting and a little patience go a long way in such a small room.

kyr_yatai_ramen_kyoto_chuka_.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac or strict gluten-free. This is a classic Kyoto-style chuka soba: wheat noodles in a pork-bone soy-sauce (shoyu) broth with back fat, and the shoyu tare almost certainly contains wheat. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodation is indicated, and as a single-operator truck-bed yatai there is no separate prep space. Avoid if you require gluten-free.
kyr_yatai_ramen_kyoto_chuka_.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. All bowls are built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy broth with back fat and are topped with chashu (pork). No vegetable or vegan broth option is offered. There is nothing on the menu suitable for a strict vegan or vegetarian diner.
kyr_yatai_ramen_kyoto_chuka_.hours_raw: ~19:00 to ~25:00 (1:00 the next day). Irregular days off. As a street stall, its operating days and location vary; the latest info is announced on Instagram.

chef_bio.background: A rare survivor of an almost-vanished Kyoto tradition: the late-night ramen yatai. Tokumitsu launched on 28 November 2023, run by a young owner out of the cargo bed of a converted kei-truck. Rather than a fixed shop, it rolls out after dark and parks at spots around the Saiin crossing, announcing each night's location on social media.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「店舗さながらの味を屋台で」 — to deliver shop-quality ramen from a food cart. The owner leans into the romance of the form: an unmarked truck under a red lantern, a handful of spots, and a warm bowl eaten outdoors on a cold night.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the 背脂チャッチャ (seabura chaccha) chuka soba — old-school Kyoto-style ramen: a pork-bone soy-sauce broth crowned with a generous shower of back fat, topped with chashu, with the salty-sharp snap of shoyu over slightly soft, chewy noodles (~780 yen). Alongside it are a lighter 昔ながらの京だし (Kyo-dashi) chuka soba and a punchy 旨辛ニンニク辛麺 (spicy garlic) bowl (~800 yen).

anecdotes.text: Because the cart roves and keeps irregular hours, regulars treat finding it as a small stroke of luck — 神出鬼没 (appearing and vanishing) is part of its charm; you track it down via its Instagram (@yatairamen_tokumitsu).
The whole appeal is a hot bowl eaten outdoors under a cold sky; one diner wrote that despite the bitter cold the warm ramen was especially comforting and delicious (寒い中体もあったまって美味しかった).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyo-soku and kyotogourmet confirm the Nov 28 2023 launch, the converted kei-truck with a young owner, the roving 神出鬼没 operation around Saiin with locations posted on Instagram, and the three bowls (背脂チャッチャ ~¥780, 昔ながらの京だし, 旨辛ニンニク辛麺 ~¥800). The exact wording of an owner quote about cold-weather ramen could not be verified, so a source-traceable diner sentiment is used instead.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single-operator truck-bed yatai serving wheat-noodle ramen in one shared pot/workspace; no separate gluten-free prep is possible and none is advertised.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broth is a pork-bone soy-sauce (shoyu) base — 「豚骨醤油のスープにたっぷりの背脂」 — and the shoyu tare typically contains wheat. Not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every bowl is pork-bone broth with back fat and chashu; there is no vegan/vegetarian option and all prep shares the pork-based broth.

cultural_comfort.note: A late-night Japanese street-cart ramen run with a young local owner and only a few spots at the truck — basic Japanese and an easygoing, go-with-the-flow attitude (it moves and keeps irregular hours) will serve you best; little to no English expected.

kyr_menshou_ichiryu_manbai_k.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The bowls are built on wheat: ramen noodles, tsukemen noodles, and mazesoba noodles are all wheat-based (the noodles even use whole-grain wheat flour for flavor), and the shoyu tare is wheat-based soy sauce. Broths are chicken and duck stock. There is no published gluten-free menu, no rice-noodle option, and no indication of allergen accommodation. A celiac diner should not eat here.
kyr_menshou_ichiryu_manbai_k.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian friendly. Every signature item is animal-based: the broth is chicken-and-duck (鶏と鴨) clear soup, toppings include chicken and pork chashu, and the mazesoba uses chicken oil and minced chashu. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu and no plant-based broth alternative.

chef_bio.background: A late-night ramen specialist in central Kyoto's Kawaramachi district, tucked into the World Building on Daikoku-cho near the Kiyamachi and Pontocho nightlife streets. The shop is part of the small Ichiryu Manbai noodle group, which also runs a Teramachi branch nearby.
chef_bio.philosophy: Care put into balance and texture: thin curly noodles cut with whole-grain wheat flour to carry more aroma, paired with a clean but assertive shoyu broth and carefully prepared toppings (chicken and pork chashu, bamboo shoots, soft egg, mitsuba/parsley).
chef_bio.specialty: A clear (清湯) double broth built on chicken and duck, finished with a crisp, sharp soy-sauce tare for the signature shoyu ramen (らぁ麺). The kitchen also turns out a tsukemen and a mazesoba that mixes thick flat noodles with chicken-oil sauce, minced chashu, red onion, and a truffle-oil-dressed egg yolk with lemon to shift the flavor partway through.

anecdotes.text: The mazesoba is described by a noodle blogger as having a sticky, clinging, oil-forward texture close to an abura-soba, brightened at the table with truffle-oil egg yolk and a squeeze of lemon.

No gluten-free menu, no dedicated prep, and as a busy mall food-court stall there is no allowance for managing cross-contamination. Avoid if you have celiac disease or a wheat allergy.
kyr_tsukemen_tetsu_aeon_mall.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The core product is built on a pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) broth, topped with chashu pork and finished with animal-derived tare; menma and noodles are cooked in shared equipment. There is no vegan or vegetarian option advertised.

chef_bio.origin: Sendagi, Tokyo (founded 2005); this branch is a Kyoto outpost of the national TETSU chain.
chef_bio.background: TETSU began in 2005 as a tiny 10-tsubo (about 33 sqm) shop in Sendagi, Tokyo, founded by Kazunori Komiya. Starting with just 3 million yen in capital, he grew it into a tsukemen brand of roughly 30 shops centered on Tokyo. This AEON Mall KYOTO branch opened on October 17, 2023, marking the brand's return to Kyoto more than a decade after its earlier Kyoto Ramen Koji shop inside the Kyoto Station Building closed in 2011.
chef_bio.philosophy: An uncompromising obsession with keeping the broth hot to the very last bite — the brand's trademark hot-stone (焼き石) service, in which a scorching stone is dropped into the dipping broth to keep it piping hot. Note that this hot-stone service is a signature of TETSU's standalone shops and is not offered at this AEON Mall food-court outlet.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) tsukemen — a triple soup of chicken bones, pork bones and bonito/mackerel — served with extra-thick straight noodles that stand up to the heavy dipping broth. Miso and spicy-miso dipping versions are also popular here, and the kitchen rounds out the menu with a chashu rice bowl and a chuka-soba.

anecdotes.text: TETSU's trademark move solves tsukemen's classic weak point of broth going lukewarm: a stone heated until scorching is dropped into the dipping broth partway through the meal so it stays piping hot until the final drop — though this hot-stone service is not available at the AEON Mall food-court branch.
Founder Kazunori Komiya turned a 3-million-yen, 10-tsubo Sendagi shop opened in 2005 into a roughly 30-location tsukemen chain.
The Kyoto branch opened in the AEON Mall KYOTO food court on October 17, 2023, returning the brand to Kyoto after its station-building shop had closed in 2011.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: pasonacareer confirms founder 小宮一哲 (b.1976), the 2005 Sendagi start with ¥3M capital and growth to ~30 shops; 1goten confirms the 焼き石 hot-stone concept and 極太ストレート麺 (no udon-flour claim); atpress confirms the Oct 17 2023 AEON Mall KYOTO opening, the triple pork-chicken-seafood broth, miso/spicy-miso versions, the 2011 closure of the Kyoto Station Building shop, and that the food-court outlet does NOT offer the hot stone.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles boiled in shared water in a single open food-court kitchen; no gluten-free handling. Not suitable for celiac diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tsukemen broth/tare uses wheat-based shoyu and miso; the noodles themselves are wheat (blended with udon flour).

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are based on pork-bone-and-seafood broth with pork chashu; no separate vegan prep area.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual mall food-court stall where you order at the counter and carry your tray, so a friendly konnichiwa and pointing at the menu is all you need.

kyr_iwasaki_tanmen.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. Tanmen is built on wheat ramen noodles in a salt (shio) tare; the broth and house salt sauce are not documented as wheat-free, and there are no gluten-free noodle or accommodation options on the menu. No allergen handling is documented. Anyone with celiac disease or wheat allergy should treat this as unsafe.
kyr_iwasaki_tanmen.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The signature tanmen is a chicken-bone and pork-based salt broth topped with stir-fried pork and vegetables; pork and a chicken/pork stock are integral to every bowl. No plant-based broth or vegetable-only version is documented. A diner could potentially ask about a vegetable-heavy customization, but the base soup is animal-derived.

chef_bio.background: Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). It is a rarity in Kyoto: a shop devoted to tanmen, a vegetable-piled salt ramen far more common in the Kanto region of eastern Japan than here in Kansai.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make-it-your-own simplicity: diners can dial the vegetables, pork, noodle quantity, garlic and spice to taste, and garlic is served on the side so each guest controls their own portion. Sides like gyoza, karaage and takana rice round out an honest, affordable bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The house tanmen is the signature: a mound of lightly stir-fried vegetables — cabbage, bean sprouts and more — over medium straight noodles in a chicken-and-pork salt (shio) broth. It arrives looking hearty and Jiro-esque, yet the soup is surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy back-fat. A pot of house chili-miso (kara-miso) sits at hand so you can stir in heat and depth gradually as you eat.

anecdotes.text: The shop offers several tanmen styles beyond the original — a shio-tonkotsu, a rich miso and a spicy version — so regulars can rotate through the lineup.
One local blogger called the proprietor very kind and admitted he came back years after his first visit because he simply could not forget the tanmen.
The bowl starts around 690 yen, keeping it genuinely budget-friendly.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the March 2023 opening in Yamashina-Ono near Ono Station in the former Shioemon space, the Kanto-style tanmen (rare in Kyoto) on a light chicken-pork shio broth, four tanmen varieties (classic/shio-tonkotsu/miso/spicy), customizable veg/pork/garlic-on-the-side/spice, kara-miso, gyoza/karaage/takana-rice sides, ~¥690, and 16 seats.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The core dish uses wheat ramen noodles in a shared salt broth; there is no published gluten-free option and the kitchen is a small single-line operation, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's tare is described as a house-made salt (shio) sauce rather than a soy-based one; however, its full composition is not published, so wheat content cannot be confirmed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetables are stir-fried together with pork, and the broth is chicken/pork based, so vegetable toppings share animal ingredients and equipment.

positives.text: Diners can customize vegetables, pork, noodle amount, garlic and spice level, with garlic served separately for portion control — useful for tailoring a bowl, though not an allergen accommodation.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly neighborhood counter-and-table shop where Japanese phrases for ordering and customizing your bowl will go a long way; English support is not documented.

kyr_dashi_ryori_jifu.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature bowl centers on house-made noodles cut from domestic wheat and egg, so the core dish contains gluten. The broth itself is a clean fish dashi (Rishiri kombu, sawara/sagoshi, bonito) seasoned with salt only and no soy sauce, which removes one common wheat source — but the wheat noodle makes this unsafe for celiacs. No dedicated gluten-free preparation is advertised; a celiac diner would need to ask directly and likely cannot be accommodated.
kyr_dashi_ryori_jifu.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. The dashi is entirely animal-based (sawara/Spanish mackerel, bonito flakes, plus kombu), and the noodles contain egg. There is no plant-based bowl on offer.

chef_bio.origin: Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto — on the city's famous Ichijoji ramen street, but a deliberate step away from the heavy-broth pack.
chef_bio.background: The shop is the latest evolution of a Kyoto noodle maker who has spent years chasing dashi rather than richness. The lineage runs from a dashi-based ramen shop, Isao (イサオ, opened 2010), which the owner renamed and reframed in 2014 as Odashi to Komugi 130 (おだしと小麦 一三〇) to put the dashi and the wheat front and center. In June 2022 the concept was distilled again into だし料理 十.
chef_bio.philosophy: The whole place is built so customers can actually understand dashi — you can watch it being made, taste it, and talk it through with the owner. Seasoning is pared back to almost nothing so the stock itself carries the bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the breakfast-only o-dashi no new-men: a clear soup built from just three things — Rishiri kombu, sawara (young Spanish mackerel / sagoshi), and bonito flakes — seasoned with a single gram of Iwate salt and no soy sauce at all. The noodles are made in-house from domestic wheat and egg, cut to roughly 1mm square and dusted with Hokkaido corn flour, then finished with hand-shaved bonito and a few pieces of salt-cured pepper.

anecdotes.text: By late afternoon the shop sheds its noodle-counter identity and becomes a dashi retail shop and small sake bar, selling drinkable dashi (nomu o-dashi) and easy dashi kits so people can take the craft home.
Tasters describe being unexpectedly moved by the bowl — 出汁のふくよかな香りとまろやかな口当たり (the rich aroma and rounded mouthfeel of the dashi genuinely move you).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: life-info and Tabelog (former name 'Odashi&Wheat isao') confirm owner Inoue, the lineage Isao (2010) -> おだしと小麦 一三〇 (2014) -> だし料理 十 (June 2022), the breakfast-only o-dashi new-men (Rishiri kombu, sawara, bonito, 1g Iwate salt, no soy; ~1mm domestic wheat-egg noodles with Hokkaido corn flour; hand-shaved bonito and salt-cured pepper), and the afternoon dashi-retail/sake-bar with nomu o-dashi and dashi kits.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The house-made noodles are cut from domestic wheat (and egg) in-house, so flour is handled on-site; a shared-kitchen wheat environment should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature dashi bowl uses no soy sauce at all — it is seasoned with about 1 gram of Iwate salt only — so the usual wheat-shoyu tare risk is absent from the broth (the wheat comes from the noodles instead).

vegan_cross_contact.text: The dashi is animal-based throughout (sawara/Spanish mackerel and bonito alongside kombu), and the noodles contain egg, so there is no clean vegan or vegetarian path.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 「利尻昆布、さわら、まぐろ節で出汁を引き」 — Rishiri kombu, sawara and まぐろ節 (dried TUNA flakes). Noodles: 「国産小麦と卵のみを使用した…自家製麺」.

positives.text: Because the owner makes and explains the dashi in front of guests, it is easy to ask exactly what is in the bowl, and the seasoning is unusually transparent: kombu, sawara, bonito, salt, and house wheat-and-egg noodles.
positives.source_wording: 「料理や小売り、情報発信を通して「出汁を知ってもらいたい」と昨年6月オープン。店主・井上さんが出汁を引く様子を見て、味わって、話を聞けば自然と出汁が身近に感じられる。」

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run dashi specialist where the proprietor talks you through the craft; some Japanese (or a translation app) goes a long way, and a quiet, curious attitude fits the room.

kyr_kyoto_kitayama_motomachi_2.gf_detail: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. The ramen uses wheat noodles, a wheat-based tamari/black soy sauce tare (sourced from a long-established Kyoto soy sauce maker), and pork/beef broth. There is no gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no indication staff accommodate gluten allergies.
kyr_kyoto_kitayama_motomachi_2.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian options. The broth is a rich black soy sauce ramen built on pork/beef bases (beef tendon is a signature), the noodles are wheat, and the tare uses wheat-containing tamari soy sauce. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Kitayama district yatai origins); founder from Kanazawa
chef_bio.background: Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen traces its roots to a street cart (yatai) that the first-generation owner — a native of Kanazawa — set up on Shinmachi-dori in Kyoto's Kitayama district roughly 50 years ago. Drawing on the rich, dark soy-sauce style of nearby Toyama Black, he built a Kyoto take on the bowl using tamari soy sauce from a long-established local soy-sauce maker. The business later moved into a permanent shop, settling at its current location in an alley off Higashinotoin in central Kyoto, where the cart's original flavor is carried on by a later (third) generation.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honor the original yatai flavor while continuing to refine it; serve until the broth is gone and then close for the day.
chef_bio.specialty: A rich black-soy-sauce ramen finished with plenty of back fat (背脂醤油らーめん), with beef-tendon ramen (牛すじらーめん) as a second signature. The defining element is a specialty tamari soy sauce of the kind used for eel sauce, sourced from a 160-year-old Kyoto soy-sauce maker.

anecdotes.text: The founder, from Kanazawa, based his recipe on the dark, bold style of Toyama Black but reinterpreted it for Kyoto using local tamari soy sauce.
The shop began as a Kitayama Shinmachi street cart about 50 years ago, and a later (third) generation continues the cart's original taste at the current shop.
The tamari soy sauce is supplied by a 160-year-old established Kyoto soy-sauce shop (Sawai) and is of the type used for eel sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site confirms the 創業50年 Kitayama Shinmachi yatai origin, a Kanazawa-born first-generation owner inspired by 富山ブラック, the specialty たまり醤油 (eel-sauce type) from a 160-year-old Kyoto maker (Sawai), the 背脂醤油らーめん (¥900) and 牛すじらーめん (¥1,100), the Higashinotoin 京町家 location, and continuation by a third generation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is built on a tamari/black soy sauce tare; tamari and standard soy sauce here are wheat-containing and central to the broth.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth and toppings are pork/beef based (beef tendon is a signature), so no item is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A cash-only, counter-style local ramen shop with no English service signaled; basic Japanese or a translation app will make ordering smoother.

kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.gf_detail: A 99-year-old Kyoto rice merchant (廣瀬米穀店, est. 1926) that sells no wheat products, with an attached café whose owner is a certified 米粉マイスター (rice-flour master) and 五ツ星お米マイスター. Because it is a food shop and rice mill rather than a certified dedicated gluten-free kitchen, celiac guests should still confirm on the day that no wheat is handled or stored on-site. In practice the entire product line is rice-based, so cross-contact risk is low.
kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.vegan_detail: The お米パン / こめやパン rice bread is fully plant-based — made only from rice, rice oil, maple, salt, rice starter (米種), yeast and water — so it is suitable for vegans (sold Wednesdays / by pre-order). The signature 米粉シフォンケーキ and its rusk contain egg and are not vegan. Small baked snacks (scones, snowballs) may contain dairy, so ask before ordering.
kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.hours_raw: 11:00-18:00. Closed Sun, Mon and holidays (rice-flour chiffon cake Tue-Sat, rice bread on Wed).
kyo_hirose_okomeya_cafe.notes: [GF] A genuinely useful stop for celiacs just south of Kyoto Station: a century-old rice merchant with an attached café where everything is 100% rice flour and the shop sells no wheat products at all. Confirm the day's baking schedule (chiffon Tue–Sat, bread Wed) and that lunch/café-gohan service is running, as it has been paused at times. Small neighborhood shop — assume cash.

chef_bio.origin: Originally from Okayama; studied fine art at a design university, then married into the third-generation Hirose rice-merchant family in Higashi-Kujo, Minami-ku, Kyoto.
chef_bio.background: 廣瀬米穀店 was founded in 昭和元年 (1926) and is now in its third generation, giving it roughly 99 years of history as a Kyoto rice merchant. Around 2014, after the shop stopped wholesaling to a large facility, an empty space opened up in the store; the owner's encounter with rice flour and the question 「米屋にしかできないことってなんだろう？」 (what can only a rice shop do?) led to the 2017 opening of the attached café, お米屋カフェ・ふぇ〜る. 廣瀬弘香 — originally from Okayama and trained in fine art before marrying into the family — holds the 五ツ星お米マイスター qualification (with the professional 'Prof' instructor grade) plus 米粉マイスター and 米粉パンマイスター certifications, and the shop is a 「五ツ星お米マイスター認定店」. The rice used is milled in-house (自家精米) from selected varieties, and all café products are made with 100% rice flour and no wheat flour or white sugar.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner wants to spread rice bread 「グルテンフリーのパンとしてではなく、生米から作る一つのおいしい食べ物として」 — not merely as gluten-free bread, but as a delicious food in its own right made from raw rice. She distinguishes 米粉パン (from rice grown for milling into flour) from her お米パン made from top-grade (一等上質米) whole rice, emphasizing the aroma and natural taste of freshly milled rice.
chef_bio.specialty: 米屋の米粉シフォンケーキ, お米パン（こめやパン）, 米粉ラスク

anecdotes.text: 2014年ごろ大型施設への卸販売を中止して店内に空きスペースが生じ、米粉との出会いから『米屋にしかできないことってなんだろう？』という問いが2017年の『お米屋カフェ・ふぇ〜る』開業につながった。
2023年に京都女性起業家賞・優秀賞、京都商工会議所主催の知恵-1グランプリ チャレンジ部門グランプリを受賞。

anecdotes.text: 運が良ければ京町家の外から職人がバウムを焼く工房の様子を眺められる。
毎週日曜14時から店頭に並ぶ『朝焼きバウム』（1カット220円）は実店舗のみの限定商品で、定番よりさらにふんわりした食感が味わえる。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式サイト・食べログ・アットプレス各リリース・KYOTOLIFE・life-info・まげわっぱブログ、および株式会社Ludicoのリリース群を総合すると、母体はイカリヤ食堂やikariya523等を運営する株式会社Ludico（代表 鳥井和機）。滋賀県産うるち米などを生米で仕入れ工房内で挽きたてに自家製粉し、グルテンフリーの米粉バウムクーヘンを焼く専門店。2023年3月29日のJR京都伊勢丹期間限定出店・オンライン販売あり。煎餅製造業由来という説は日本語一次情報では裏付けられなかった。

gf_cross_contamination.text: 焼き菓子の製造ラインは自家製粉の米粉のみで小麦粉を使用しない専門工房のため、製品自体の小麦クロスコンタミ・リスクは低い。
個人ブログでは『メニューはすべて米粉を使ったグルテンフリー』と報告されているが、店奥のイートインで供する飲み物・付け合わせに小麦品がないかは公式には未確認。

vegan_cross_contact.text: バウムクーヘンは卵・乳(バター)を含むため、ヴィーガン品との交差接触管理に関する情報はなく、そもそもヴィーガン提供品が確認できない。

staff_allergy_handling.text: 米菓職人が自家製粉した米粉で丁寧に焼き上げると明記されるが、個別の小麦アレルギー対応プロトコルの記載は見当たらない。

positives.text: 専門店として全焼き菓子が米粉ベースの小麦不使用で、グルテンフリーの土産・スイーツとして京都のGFガイドでも紹介されている。
生米を工房内で自家製粉するなど原材料管理にこだわり、JR京都伊勢丹でもグルテンフリーバウムとして販売実績がある。

chef_bio.chef_name: うのゆきこ (Uno Yukiko) — 豆乳パティシエ / soy-milk patissier
chef_bio.background: Uno Yukiko styles herself as 「世界で唯一の豆乳パティシエ」 (the world's only soy-milk patissier) and opened Mushiyashinai in Ichijoji around 2006. In December 2009 an encounter with a boy who had 23 food allergies (23品目の食物アレルギー) pushed her to develop allergy-friendly cakes made from 米粉 and 豆乳 rather than wheat and dairy, and by 2020 she completed a cake free of 29 allergens (29品目のアレルゲン不使用). In October 2023 she renovated both the production factory and the shop expressly to convert the whole operation to gluten-free. This Ichijoji patisserie is a distinct venue from the operator's soy-milk ramen line (branded 'UNO RAMEN'); the sweets shop, not the ramen, is the celiac-relevant location.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「すべての人を笑顔にするために」— pursuing 食のバリアフリー (barrier-free food) across social, health and religious dietary needs; plant-based, gluten-free, allergen-conscious baking.
chef_bio.specialty: Soy-milk & rice-flour cakes, 焼き菓子, 豆乳プリン, ブリュレ, おから (soy-pulp) sweets and light savory items
